meta.audience: Readers of the abridgment; Mormon's brethren, the Lamanites
meta.location: Unstated; Mormon writes near the end of the Nephite nation

world_behind.title: A thousand-year jump, unannounced
world_behind.text: The previous page ended with Amaleki around 130 BC. This one opens with a man watching the destruction of his nation five centuries after Christ. The reader crosses a millennium between two chapters, and the only signal is the change of name.

world_behind.title: The wise purpose, unresolved on both ends
world_behind.text: Nephi was told to make the small plates "for a wise purpose" he did not know. Mormon includes them for a wise purpose he also does not know — verse 7 says so outright. Two men separated by a thousand years both act on an instruction neither of them understands.

world_behind.title: An archival find
world_behind.text: Verse 3 has Mormon searching records already delivered into his hands and discovering these plates. The abridgment was finished down to Benjamin before he knew they existed. What the reader has been reading for six books is presented here as something its compiler stumbled on late.

world_behind.title: False prophets tried and punished
world_behind.text: Verses 15 and 16 report false Christs, false prophets, preachers, and teachers, all "punished according to their crimes." Religious offense is handled as a legal matter by the state, which is how the ancient Near East generally handled it, and the record does not describe the proceedings.

world_behind.title: A king who fights, judges, and preaches
world_behind.text: Benjamin swings a sword in verse 13, presides over punishments in verses 15 and 16, and labors with prophets to establish peace in verse 18. The portrait is of an office that has not yet separated its military, judicial, and religious functions.

words.text: An impersonal construction — it seems to me — and the King James Bible does not use it this way. Mormon says it supposeth him that his son will watch the nation die. The grammar holds the conclusion at arm's length, which is a strange thing to do with a sentence about your own child.

A shortening that preserves the substance. Mormon uses it of his own work, which makes him the first writer in the record to name his method. Everything from here to the end of the book is filtered through one man's judgment about what to keep, and he says so before the reader reaches it.

Selected, and therefore valuable — the word carries both. Mormon keeps the small plates because they are choice unto him and says he knows they will be choice unto his brethren. The allegory in Jacob 5 used it of the best ground in the vineyard. It is the record's word for what one keeps when there is no room for everything.

phrases.term: may God grant that he may survive them, that he may write somewhat
phrases.text: A father's prayer for his son's survival, and the reason given is not that the son may live but that he may write. Mormon has already concluded his people will be destroyed entirely. What he asks for is a witness who outlasts them, and Moroni does.

phrases.term: I searched among the records which had been delivered into my hands, and I found these plates
phrases.text: The discovery is reported as ordinary archival work. He was going through what he already had. The small plates — Nephi's, Jacob's, and the rest — enter the compiled record because a man doing an inventory noticed them, and the record says so plainly.

phrases.term: the things which are upon these plates pleasing me, because of the prophecies of the coming of Christ
phrases.text: The stated reason for keeping them, and it is a reader's reason rather than a historian's. Mormon is selecting on content he finds compelling, and the next clause explains why: he can see which of the prophecies have already been fulfilled from where he stands.

phrases.term: I cannot write the hundredth part of the things of my people
phrases.text: Jacob's formula, five hundred years later, now in the mouth of the man compiling the whole thing. The complaint that began as a frustration about metal has become the standing condition of the record, and from here forward it governs everything.

phrases.term: I do this for a wise purpose; for thus it whispereth me
phrases.text: To whisper is to speak below normal volume, and the verb measures the strength of the impression exactly: enough to act on, not enough to explain. This is the closest the record comes to describing its own composition as guided without explanation. Mormon gives a reason he cannot state, attributes it to the Spirit, and immediately concedes the limits of his knowledge. Nephi had been given the same instruction in the same words.

phrases.term: I do not know all things; but the Lord knoweth all things which are to come
phrases.text: An admission placed in the middle of an editorial decision. Mormon is deciding what will survive, and he says he is working without full information. The sentence is a compiler describing his own position accurately.

phrases.term: that they may once again be a delightsome people
phrases.text: "Delightsome" means pleasing to look upon, and the record uses it of peoples rather than things; the phrase that carries the weight here is "once again," which makes the petition a restoration rather than a description. This is Mormon's prayer for the Lamanites, offered by a man whose nation they are destroying. The petition is for their restoration and not for his people's survival, and it is the only thing in the chapter he calls a prayer.

phrases.term: out of which my people and their brethren shall be judged at the great and last day
phrases.text: The plates given a judicial function. Preservation is requested in the previous clause and justified here, and the justification is that the writing will be read against both peoples at a final accounting. Memory is not the reason offered. Evidence is.

phrases.term: he did fight with the strength of his own arm, with the sword of Laban
phrases.text: Two strengths named together, and the second is a relic. Nephi took the blade in a dark street; Benjamin swings it in a war roughly four hundred and seventy years later. Across four books it has been a weapon, a pattern for an armory, a line in a eulogy, and now a king's blade. The record never explains how it was kept, only that it was.

phrases.term: there had been false Christs, and their mouths had been shut
phrases.text: The phrase is a New Testament one and the treatment is judicial. Mouths shut, punishment according to crimes — the account is administrative rather than theological, and no argument with the false Christs is recorded, only the outcome.

phrases.term: they did use much sharpness because of the stiffneckedness of the people
phrases.text: Sharpness is severity of speech — Paul uses it of what he hopes not to need, and Lehi used it defending Nephi to his brothers. Cause and method here, stated without apology. The record has defended harsh preaching before, at the end of Enos. Here it is attributed to many holy men at once and made a feature of Benjamin's reign rather than one prophet's temperament.

phrases.term: by laboring with all the might of his body and the faculty of his whole soul
phrases.text: Body and soul named separately and both spent. The phrase occurs once in scripture. What it describes is not a victory or a revelation but the establishment of peace, and the labor is shared with prophets in the same sentence.

verses.label: v. 1–2
verses.title: Mormon, at the end
verses.text: He is handing the record to his son, he has watched almost all of his people destroyed, and he expects Moroni to watch the rest. The prayer is that his son survive long enough to write. Two verses, and they are the darkest opening of any book in the record.

verses.label: v. 3–6
verses.title: What he found and why he kept it
verses.text: The abridgment was already made down to Benjamin; searching his own holdings he found these plates; the prophecies of Christ pleased him and he could see them fulfilled; he cannot write the hundredth part; he keeps them because they are choice. The compiler's reasoning, given in full.

verses.label: v. 7–9
verses.title: A whisper, and an admission
verses.text: A wise purpose, a whisper, an admission that he does not know all things, a prayer that the Lamanites be delightsome again, and a statement that he will now proceed from the plates of Nephi. The center of the chapter is a man acting on an instruction he cannot explain.

verses.label: v. 10–11
verses.title: The chain of custody, completed
verses.text: Amaleki to Benjamin, Benjamin to the kings, the kings down the generations, and at last into Mormon's hands. Then the prayer that they be preserved and the reason: two nations will be judged out of what is written on them.

verses.label: v. 12–14
verses.title: Benjamin at war
verses.text: Contentions at home, Lamanite armies down from the land of Nephi, the king fighting with his own arm and with the sword of Laban, and the enemy driven out of all the lands of their inheritance. Three verses of national survival, told without any detail about cost.

verses.label: v. 15–17
verses.title: Benjamin and the false teachers
verses.text: False Christs, false prophets, false preachers and teachers, all punished; much contention and many dissensions; and then the description of the king himself — holy, reigning in righteousness, with many holy men speaking with power and using much sharpness.

verses.label: v. 18
verses.title: Peace, established once more
verses.text: One verse for the outcome, and it credits the king's body and soul and the prophets together. The chapter that began with the end of a nation ends with a king restoring order five hundred years earlier, which is the point at which the abridgment proper picks up.

chapter.title: The record explains its own construction and does not hide the seam
chapter.text: Mormon stops the narrative to say what he found, when he found it, why he kept it, and where the next section comes from. No other compiler in scripture is this explicit about the join, and the explanation is placed exactly where the sources change.

chapter.title: Two men act on the same unexplained instruction a thousand years apart
chapter.text: Nephi made the small plates for a wise purpose he did not know; Mormon attaches them for a wise purpose he does not know either. The record presents the whole arrangement as something neither participant could see the reason for.

chapter.title: The compiler admits the limits of his own knowledge
chapter.text: Verse 7 has him saying he does not know all things in the middle of the most consequential editorial choice in the book. It is an unusual sentence for an editor to preserve about himself, and he preserves it without softening.

chapter.title: The plates are described as evidence, not as memory
chapter.text: Verse 11 makes the writing something both peoples are answerable to at the last day. That is a legal function, and it is a stronger reason for preservation than any the record has given before — stronger than the family, the genealogy, or the prophecies.

chapter.title: Mormon's only recorded prayer here is for his enemies
chapter.text: His nation is being destroyed by the Lamanites, and what he asks God for is that the Lamanites come again to the knowledge of God and be a delightsome people. Nothing is asked for the Nephites except that his son outlive them.

chapter.title: Benjamin is introduced by what he does, not by what he says
chapter.text: He fights, he punishes, he labors, and he establishes peace, all before the reader hears a word from him. The great sermon comes two chapters later, and this chapter is what earns it a hearing.

chapter.title: The chapter is written from the end and set at the beginning
chapter.text: Mormon knows how the story finishes and is placing a document at its middle. Everything in it about preservation, judgment, and surviving witnesses is written by someone who has already seen the outcome, which is why the tone is settled rather than hopeful.

applications.title: Act on the whisper you cannot justify
applications.text: Mormon kept the plates on an impression he could not explain, and said so. When something small and unaccountable seems right, the chapter's model is to do it and note honestly that you do not know why.

applications.title: Say what you do not know
applications.text: He made a consequential decision and recorded that he lacked full information. In your own accounts — a report, a recommendation, a piece of advice — name the limits of what you actually know.

applications.title: Search what you already have
applications.text: Mormon found the most valuable thing in his archive by going through material already in his possession. Before acquiring something new, inventory what is already on your shelf.

applications.title: Pray for the ones doing the damage
applications.text: Mormon's one prayer here is for the people destroying his nation. Name someone who has cost you something, and ask for their good specifically rather than generally.

applications.title: Write so someone can be judged fairly
applications.text: The plates were kept as evidence. When you record something contentious, write it so that it would still be fair if read by everyone involved.

applications.title: Spend body and soul on peace
applications.text: Benjamin's effort is described in both registers, and what he produced was order rather than victory. Ask what the equivalent labor looks like in a conflict you are inside of.

questions.text: If I could ask one thing for the person who comes after me, what would it be?
What is already in my possession that I have never actually looked through?
When did I last act on an impression I could not explain, and what happened?
Who is costing me something right now, and could I pray for their good and mean it?
If what I write were read at a final accounting, what would I want to change about how I write it?
Am I using sharpness where patience is called for, or patience where sharpness is?
